title: Join or add?
intro: `+` does two jobs: between two numbers it adds, and the moment either side is a `String` it joins. Java works left to right, one `+` at a time. You are the `+`.

rounds.right: Left to right: the two numbers were added first, and only then did a `String` turn up and join. It prints {shown}.

why.add: One side is a `String` ({str}), so this `+` joins: {num} is turned into text and the two are stuck together.
why.join: Both sides are `int`s ({l} and {r}), so this `+` is plain addition. Joining only starts once a `String` is involved.

rounds.right: The `String` came first, so every `+` after it joins: it prints {shown}, not a sum.

why.add: The left side is already a `String` ({str}), so this `+` joins: the result of the last step was text, and text plus a number is text.
why.join: Both sides are `int`s ({l} and {r}), so this `+` adds.

rounds.prompt: Brackets first: Java works out a bracketed group before it can use it. Which `+` comes first, and does it add or join?
rounds.right: The brackets were worked out first, while both sides were still numbers, so it prints {shown}. Without them it would join the digits one by one.

why.add: One side is a `String` ({str}), so this `+` joins: {num} becomes text.
why.join: Inside the brackets both sides are `int`s ({l} and {r}), and Java works that out before it looks outside: it adds.

rounds.prompt: `String.format` fills each placeholder with the next argument, in order. What does it return?
rounds.right: `%s` took the String, `%.2f` the double rounded to two decimal places, and `%d` the int: the colours show which argument went where.

why.String.format.unrounded: `%.2f` shows exactly two digits after the decimal point, rounded; it doesn't print all of the double's digits.
why.String.format.cut: `%.2f` rounds to the nearest hundredth: it doesn't just chop off the digits after the second one.
why.*: Each placeholder takes the next argument in order: `%s` a String, `%.2f` a double with two decimal places, `%d` an int.

rounds.prompt: `String.join` takes the separator first, then the pieces. What does it return?
rounds.right: The separator goes between the pieces, never before the first or after the last: three pieces, two separators.

why.String.join.after: The separator only goes between pieces: there is nothing after the last one for it to separate.
why.String.join.around: The separator only goes between pieces, never at the ends.
why.String.join.none: The first argument, `"-"`, is the separator: it goes between every pair of pieces.
